newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Netherlands 2, Belgium 0 in corporate tax war.
newsitem.headline: Netherlands 2, Belgium 0 in corporate tax war.

text.p: With the departure of corporate finance centres of two Dutch companies from Belgium, the Netherlands has scored its first points in a battle to bring tax refugees back home.
Dutch chemicals group DSM and Dutch food and drinks group Koninklijke Bolswessanen announced on Thursday plans to move their Belgian corporate finance activities back to the Netherlands.
"The fiscal advantages that are offered in Belgium have now also become available in the Netherlands," a Bolswessanen spokeswoman at the group's Dutch headquarters told Reuters.
Belgian tax specialists said they were not surprised by the two departures and expected more would follow.

"One can hope for tax harmonisation in Europe, but the reality is that there is fierce competition (on the tax front) between European countries," Belgian Economics Ministry adviser Philippe Lambot told Reuters.
Last year, the Dutch government passed a new corporate tax law, effective from 1997, aimed at enticing foreign-based financing units of Dutch companies back to the Netherlands.
Belgian tax officials say the law was aimed mainly at Belgium's so-called coordination centres -- fiscally advantaged finance centres for multinational companies.

Coordination centres, among other advantages, pay no tax on financial income and only have to pay a small flat-rate tax of about four million Belgian francs ($115,000) per year. They typically raise money on financial markets to lend it to other companies within a group. The interest earned on these loans is tax-free.

Currently there are about 250 active coordination centres in Belgium, of which about 30 are Dutch. Only multinational companies with turnover of at least 10 billion francs ($290 million) qualify. Each centre must employ at least 10 people.

"The Dutch law was aimed at making countries like Belgium and Ireland less attractive for Dutch companies. The move was part of the tax competition between the two countries," Patrick Kelley, partner at law firm De Bandt, van Hecke & Lagae said.

Kelley added that, despite the Dutch law change, Belgium still had the most advantageous tax regime for financing companies in Europe and said that he did not expect any of the numerous U.S., Scandinavian or other foreign coordination centres to move shop to the Netherlands.

But other observers said the new Dutch law puts strong pressure on Dutch companies to move by raising doubts about the fiscal status of profit transfers between Belgian coordination centres and their Dutch parent firms.

"There is not much point in enjoying zero tax in Belgium when the coordination centre's dividends to the parent company become part of its group taxable income. The new Dutch law is very dubious on that aspect," one specialist said.
A source close to Bolswessanen agreed. "One of the reasons for our move is that we want to get rid of a tax risk."
Not everyone in Belgium would be unhappy to see the coordination centres go.

"I regret that our finance minister, under the guise of competitive fiscal dumping between neighbouring countries, is such a staunch defender of coordination centres," Ecologist Party deputy Jean-Pierre Viseur said in a parliamentary budget debate last June.
